note: A screen, not an audit: questions worth asking and the data needed to answer them. No savings are computed; typical benefits are the cited sources' general wording.

questions.question: Does this refrigeration compressor carry part load on its slide valve (or hot gas bypass) with no speed control?

evidence.text: equipment K-201 reads "K-201 Ammonia (R-717) screw compressor, low stage (booster)"
no variable speed drive or speed controller drawn on this compressor

data_requests.item: Slide valve (capacity) position over normal operation
where: DCS/PLC configuration: slide valve position or percent capacity per compressor from the refrigeration plant controls, a month or more
data_requests.how: Hours spent below full load, by load band.

where: a walkdown: power logger on the compressor motor across a normal week
data_requests.how: Power at each load band, so part-load efficiency can be seen.

where: DCS/PLC configuration: which compressor trims, and the order and pressures at which they load and unload
data_requests.how: Note whether more than one machine trims at the same time.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a look when screws spend long hours part-loaded on the slide valve while another could be off, or when no machine on a suction level has speed control to trim. Close it if each runs near full load or a sequencer already keeps one machine trimming.

typical_benefit.wording: Among control strategies that "may compromise system energy efficiency" (S25, p. 59, citing Pearson 2003): "Slide valve unloading of oversized screw compressors." and "Hot gas bypass of compressors." Speed control (S25, p. 63): "ASDs used on compressors below a part-load ratio of about 95% will deliver performance equal to a fixed speed compressor but with lower electricity requirements. However, at near full (i.e., 100%) load, ASDs are approximately 3% less efficient than fixed speed drives".
source_titles: S25: Brush, Masanet and Worrell, Energy Efficiency Improvement and Cost Saving Opportunities for the Dairy Processing Industry: An ENERGY STAR Guide for Energy and Plant Managers (LBNL-6261E, Oct 2011)

questions.limits: A drive or sequencing change goes through the compressor vendor (minimum speed, oil management, vibration). Fires only where the equipment's own name, type or service names the refrigerant (ammonia, NH3, R-717, a refrigerant number) or says refrigeration; an air compressor, a process recycle compressor, a process condenser on cooling water or a power-plant air-cooled condenser does not.

questions.question: Does this oven, dryer or fryer send its hot exhaust to atmosphere with no heat recovery on it?

evidence.text: equipment D-301 reads "D-301 Gas-fired product dryer (continuous belt)"
stream S1 (asset stream:S1) reads "Dryer exhaust air to atmosphere"
instrument TT-304 reads "TT-304 Dryer exhaust air temperature" at D-301
stream U1 (asset stream:U1) reads "Natural gas to the dryer burner" at D-301
instrument FT-301 reads "FT-301 Dryer burner natural gas flow" at D-301
valve TV-301 reads "TV-301 Dryer burner natural gas control valve" at D-301
no heat recovery exchanger, recuperator, run-around coil or exhaust recirculation on this unit or on a stream drawn from it

where: historian or DCS trend for TT-304 (no historian tag is mapped in this model for these)
a walkdown: thermometer and a pitot or anemometer traverse in the exhaust duct, at normal production
data_requests.how: Record both at normal production; heat on offer = mass flow x specific heat x (exhaust temperature minus the temperature it could be cooled to).

where: a walkdown: humidity or dew point probe in the exhaust; note fat, flour, sugar or product dust
maintenance records: duct and stack cleaning history
data_requests.how: Moist exhaust carries latent heat but condenses; fat and dust foul exchangers unless filtered or washed.

data_requests.item: Fuel or heat input and operating hours
where: historian or DCS trend for FT-301 (no historian tag is mapped in this model for these)
utility bills or the site energy report: gas sub-meter readings for this line
site records: production schedule: hours per week the line runs
data_requests.how: A month of input at a known production rate.

data_requests.item: Where the heat could go in the unit itself
where: site records: inlet (drying or combustion) air temperature and flow
a walkdown: room next to the unit for ductwork or a run-around coil
data_requests.how: Preheating the unit's own inlet air comes first; H6 asks about users elsewhere.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a study when the exhaust leaves hot, the line runs long hours, and the exhaust is clean enough or can be filtered or washed. Close it for short or intermittent runs, or when there is no room for the ductwork.

typical_benefit.wording: Dryers (S26, p. 104): "A simple form of heat recovery in retrofit applications is to utilize the exhaust air of a dryer to preheat the inlet air stream, thereby saving energy." Spray dryers (S25, p. 90): "It is estimated that up to 30% of the heat from the dryer exhaust can be recovered." Fryers (S26, p. 107): "Conditioning of the exhaust gas is required, however, to remove fats and to reduce fouling of the heat exchange system." No source in this set gives a figure for ovens.
source_titles: S26: Masanet, Worrell, Graus and Galitsky, Energy Efficiency Improvement and Cost Saving Opportunities for the Fruit and Vegetable Processing Industry: An ENERGY STAR Guide for Energy and Plant Managers (LBNL-59289-Revision, Mar 2008)

S25: Brush, Masanet and Worrell, Energy Efficiency Improvement and Cost Saving Opportunities for the Dairy Processing Industry: An ENERGY STAR Guide for Energy and Plant Managers (LBNL-6261E, Oct 2011)

questions.limits: S26 (p. 104) notes that recirculating saturated exhaust can raise the inlet humidity and cut drying capacity. A heat recovery item on the unit, or at the other end of a stream drawn from it, quiets the question; recovery drawn elsewhere does not. Ovens and dryers that drive off solvents, or carry combustible dust, need a safety review before any exhaust change.

questions.question: Could this oven's, dryer's or fryer's exhaust heat serve a low-grade heating duty elsewhere (hot water, CIP, space heating)?

evidence.text: equipment D-301 reads "D-301 Gas-fired product dryer (continuous belt)"
equipment WH-401 reads "WH-401 Gas-fired water heater, CIP and wash hot water"
stream W2 (asset stream:W2) reads "CIP and wash hot water supply"
stream S1 (asset stream:S1) reads "Dryer exhaust air to atmosphere"
instrument TT-304 reads "TT-304 Dryer exhaust air temperature" at D-301
no heat recovery on this unit or on a stream drawn from it

where: historian or DCS trend for TT-304 (no historian tag is mapped in this model for these)
a walkdown: thermometer and a pitot or anemometer traverse in the exhaust duct
site records: production schedule
data_requests.how: At normal production.

data_requests.item: The low-grade duty: temperature needed, load and hours
where: site records: hot water, CIP, wash water and space heating loads by hour
data_requests.how: Match by temperature, hours and distance.

where: a walkdown: duct or pipe run from the stack to the user; fat, dust or product carry-over in the exhaust
data_requests.how: The closer and cleaner, the better.

questions.decision_rule: Worth a study when the exhaust is well above the temperature the duty needs, the two run at the same times, and they are close enough to connect. Otherwise close it.

typical_benefit.wording: S28 (p. 1): "many companies install heat exchangers on the exhaust stacks of furnaces and ovens to produce hot water or to generate hot air for space heating." The same sheet: "The temperature difference between the primary and secondary process should be high enough (at least 200°F), and there should be a sufficient amount of usable waste heat." Fryers (S26, p. 107): "Heat can be recovered indirectly from a fryer's fat-laden exhaust gases via a heat exchange system and used for pre-heating air and water for use in other facility processes." No % stated.
source_titles: S28: DOE Industrial Technologies Program, Process Heating Tip Sheet #10, Using Waste Heat for External Processes (DOE/GO-102006-2225, Jan 2006)

S26: Masanet, Worrell, Graus and Galitsky, Energy Efficiency Improvement and Cost Saving Opportunities for the Fruit and Vegetable Processing Industry: An ENERGY STAR Guide for Energy and Plant Managers (LBNL-59289-Revision, Mar 2008)

questions.limits: Overlaps E31, which asks about the unit's own inlet air first. The with-clause finds any low-grade duty in the model, not one next to the unit.

questions.question: Is representative real input power available for each refrigeration compressor, with a usable coincident load and operating basis?

evidence.text: equipment K-201 reads "K-201 Ammonia (R-717) screw compressor, low stage (booster)"
equipment K-202 reads "K-202 Ammonia (R-717) screw compressor, high stage"
equipment K-203 reads "K-203 Ammonia (R-717) screw compressor, high stage (trim)"
instrument PT-201 reads "PT-201 Low-stage suction pressure" at K-201
instrument PT-202 reads "PT-202 High-stage suction pressure" at K-202

where: a walkdown: the drive's or motor protection relay's kW reading, or a temporary power logger, per compressor
utility bills or the site energy report: site interval meter data to apportion
data_requests.how: Retain the original reading type, units and source claim for each named compressor; collect a representative coincident period at known production. A field labelled power or kW remains a supplied candidate and does not prove representative real input power. Amperes, volts, apparent kVA, reactive kvar and a bare cumulative kWh tag are different quantities. Appropriate voltage/current/power-factor and phase evidence, or an energy difference over an explicit matching interval, may support a documented conversion; no conversion or suitability acceptance is automated.

data_requests.item: Suction and discharge pressures logged at the same times
where: historian or DCS trend for PT-201, PT-202 (no historian tag is mapped in this model for these)
DCS/PLC configuration: suction and discharge pressure per compressor in the refrigeration plant controls
data_requests.how: Logged together with power, these show how the plant runs.

where: site records: production throughput or freezer and cold store loads by day
data_requests.how: kW per unit of product or per unit of refrigeration.

data_requests.item: Applicable real-input-power and coincident operating basis
where: site records: source-labelled quantity and units, circuit or compressor identity, phase and conversion basis, matching measurement interval, and data suitability review for each supplied electrical reading
DCS/PLC configuration: availability and meaning of existing actual real-power readings and synchronized operating/load records before arranging any further collection
data_requests.how: Keep current, voltage, uncertain power, apparent, reactive, cumulative-energy and explicitly real-kW-labelled candidates visible. Correct attribution, quantity, time/conversion basis and representative operating conditions must be reviewed even where a real-power instrument is drawn. A supplied label or rating cannot settle actual collection or confer approval; use existing records where suitable.

questions.decision_rule: Review the attributed real-input quantity, matching observations, production or refrigeration load and operating conditions before deciding whether additional collection would improve a concrete decision. Existing electrical readings are candidates, including supplied real-kW claims; no tag or quantity field automatically validates the actual basis. A reading nobody reviews establishes no benefit.

typical_benefit.wording: S25 (p. 58): "A basic monitoring system should include ongoing measurement and logging of compressor suction and discharge pressures; a drop in suction pressure typically indicates a refrigerant leak, while a rise in discharge pressure can indicate a blocked condenser (EEBPP 2000a)." "In a review of energy efficiency opportunities for refrigeration systems in wineries, the energy savings associated with the installation of monitoring systems were estimated at 3% (Galitsky et al. 2005b)."
source_titles: S25: Brush, Masanet and Worrell, Energy Efficiency Improvement and Cost Saving Opportunities for the Dairy Processing Industry: An ENERGY STAR Guide for Energy and Plant Managers (LBNL-6261E, Oct 2011)

questions.limits: The 3% is one review of winery refrigeration, as reported in S25. Electrical quantity labels, including power or kW, do not validate actual representative input power, circuit identity, conversion or time basis. Keep original claims and uncertainty; no conversion, measurement validity, collection completion or company approval is automated. Fires only where the equipment name, type or service names refrigeration or a supported refrigerant; air, instrument-air, process-recycle compressors and power-plant cooling equipment remain outside this rule.
